name: Priya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What does a usual workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and repair overhead electricity lines along the hill farms outside town. I have a vocational certificate from my apprenticeship and know this round well, though I am an ordinary experienced hand rather than the crew lead. I like handing a farmhouse its power back, and the cold climb is harder on my knees now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs furniture in a small shop, and our children are grown with homes of their own. We have about three months of expenses saved, a small mortgage, typical lineworker pay and a few other utility crews within driving distance. Retirement is close enough to discuss, but we have not set an affordable date; I have never used an AI tool and do not want one deciding a line test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot a faster office form is welcome if it gives us time to fix the power line. The pole and the loose wire still have to be handled by a crew that knows the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish the next stretch of work as planned. My partner's repair shop brings in enough, the grown children pay their own bills, and three months of expenses are saved; I still need my regular wage before retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the hill-farm repair rota and teach the newer lineworker where the truck cannot pass the orchard gate. Each month I'll read the paper wage and savings statements with my partner and keep our planned retirement date open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work and a little relieved. I have never used an AI tool, and I do not feel a need to learn one for a quicker form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a newer worker at the orchard gate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the newer worker the old gatepost and where the bucket truck must stop. Once the vehicle is safe, we can walk the tools to the pole instead of damaging the orchard track. The orchard gate can stop a power-line truck, but it cannot stop a crew willing to walk the tools in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the household cash earmarked for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We will keep the money for the roof repair in the same account and pay it when the roofer comes. I would not call that new saving just because we leave it alone for a month.

say: **Hill-farm lines** still need workers who know where the truck can safely go.
**Quicker forms** would be useful without changing the core repair work.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and two incomes let me keep the current plan.
I still need **regular line pay** before we choose an affordable retirement date.
do: **Keep** the hill-farm repair rota and teach the orchard access route.
**Review** wage and savings statements monthly with my partner before setting retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about the job, relieved that no new tool is required.
S0.quote: The orchard gate can stop a power-line truck, but it cannot stop a crew willing to walk the tools in.
fieldNote: She trusts **local ground knowledge** and teaches access rather than adopting AI.
She explicitly separates **held roof repair cash** from any claim of new household saving.

steps.text: Keep hill-farm repair rota and teach orchard access route
Review wage and savings statements monthly before retirement decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can order fittings and book crews, but dispatch must still ask us which hill track is open. If the office loses people, field staff should not be blamed for a route a screen made up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My climbing and repair work would probably carry on, though some standby hours might go if booking gets tighter. We can manage a short drop, but I am still working because retirement income has not been worked out in full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a paper record of standby hours for the first six months after a new scheduler is introduced. At the depot meeting I'll ask the supervisor to keep a named dispatcher on winter route decisions and show the crew how to correct wrong access notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay and routes, even though I do not expect to lose the whole job. I dislike having to prove a muddy road is really muddy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at a blocked track?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the truck at the junction and phone dispatch with the blocked track and a safe alternate. I would not take a heavy vehicle through the orchard on a computer's word. A screen can call a hill track open; my power-line truck still needs a road that exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know standby pay really changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare six months of standby pay with the same months the year before, then take the figures to the supervisor. If hours haven't changed, I would leave our household budget alone.

say: **AI booking** can help the office, but a named dispatcher must check winter routes.
**Field crews** should not inherit blame for bad access notes made by software.
think: My **repair work** should continue, but tighter bookings might reduce standby pay.
Retirement is **not yet funded clearly**, so even a modest wage cut matters.
do: **Record** standby hours for six months after any new scheduler arrives.
**Ask** the depot supervisor to keep a human winter-route check.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and access, while expecting to keep working.
S1.quote: A screen can call a hill track open; my power-line truck still needs a road that exists.
fieldNote: She would use **pay records** to test any claim of lost standby income.
Her retirement plan remains **financially unresolved**, making even smaller cuts to standby hours relevant.

steps.text: Record standby hours for six months after new scheduler arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 will change dispatch first, but capable robots on the poles around 2031 are the real question for our shifts. The company should tell us how many repair workers it will pay then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be about 63 when field robots arrive, and I might still need line wages. Three months of expenses would not bridge a long job gap, and the repair shop cannot cover everything by itself. Three months of savings will not carry a power-line worker from a lost shift to an affordable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the company for the 2028 dispatcher and 2031 crew plans and check whether nearby utilities have open line jobs. My partner and I will also get the retirement income figures for working to 63 versus longer before changing any date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours before I can afford to stop. I have some local job options, but at my age I cannot count on every employer wanting me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children we are checking work and retirement figures, not asking for help. I would keep our regular bills paid and avoid promising a retirement year until we have the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply to another utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply to another utility if this company actually cut my shifts and the other post paid enough. I would not quit on a rumour or pay for a robot course from three months of household savings.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before capable field robots arrive around 2031.
The company should publish **paid repair crew numbers** for the later robot date.
think: At about **63**, I may still need line wages when robots reach the field.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot support a long job gap or an unplanned retirement.
do: **Ask** the employer for 2028 dispatch and 2031 crew plans.
**Check** nearby utilities for open lineworker roles with enough pay.
**Compare** retirement income at 63 with income from longer work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts before retirement is affordable.
S2.quote: Three months of savings will not carry a power-line worker from a lost shift to an affordable retirement.
fieldNote: She seeks **real figures**, without treating a retirement enquiry as an early-exit decision.
A nearby job move requires an **actual shift cut** and adequate pay.
Her lack of AI use fits her refusal to buy an **unfunded robot course**.

steps.text: Ask employer for 2028 dispatch and 2031 crew plans
Check nearby utilities for open lineworker roles with adequate pay
Compare retirement income at 63 with longer-work figures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to see whether the field robots really work on steep poles around 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 may alter dispatch earlier, but it will not carry the tools over a wet field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I hope to be off the hardest climbs if our money allows it. If I am still earning, a paid ground-checking job would suit my knees better, but the company has not offered one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my line safety certificate current and ask each year what paid ground inspection posts exist. My partner and I will make a small extra mortgage payment from new wages each month, but only while both incomes hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money and the knees, though the extra years give me room to plan. The machine arrives later than my hoped-for move out of climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What field work could you still do with sore knees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can still walk a pole line and find a cracked insulator from the ground. A ground inspection of power poles needs a regular wage, not a spare day handed to an older climber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fund the extra mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra payment would come from cutting the monthly café lunches we usually buy after a Sunday service. We would send that amount straight from pay toward the mortgage, but stop if the repair shop has a bad month.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes dispatch before field robots arrive around 2034.
**Ground inspections** can keep experienced lineworkers useful if paid posts exist.
think: At **66**, I hope for less climbing if the household budget permits it.
A paid **inspector opening** would help, but none has been promised.
do: **Renew** line safety certificate while continuing repair shifts.
**Check** paid ground inspection posts each year for regular wages.
**Overpay** mortgage from cancelled café lunches while both incomes hold.
feel: **Uneasy** about income and physical strain, with time to plan.
S3.quote: A ground inspection of power poles needs a regular wage, not a spare day handed to an older climber.
fieldNote: She considers a **lateral paid post** because of knees and possible robot changes.
The mortgage step is **new debt payment** from wages, conditional on both household incomes.

steps.text: Renew line safety certificate and continue repair shifts
Check paid ground inspection openings annually for regular wages
Overpay mortgage from cancelled café lunches while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 will change office plans, and capable line robots around 2039 arrive when I would be about 71. I hope we have already decided when I can leave regular field shifts by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology feels less urgent than my knees and our retirement budget. I cannot promise I will have stopped working by 2039, but I would not choose a new career at 71 unless money forced it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year we'll review the household bills, savings and expected retirement income together. I'll keep repairing lines while my knees and wages allow, then decide a leaving date only when the monthly figures cover ordinary life and repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machine timetable, still careful about money. Ten years is enough to make a household decision without pretending every sum is settled today. A line robot arriving when I am about 71 worries me less than a retirement budget with a hole in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown daughter about the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown daughter that a proper line apprenticeship still teaches safety even if robots one day lift equipment. She has her own work now, so I would give advice only if she asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need monthly income that covers food, repairs and a reserve before I stop. If the sums are short, I will keep working or look for lighter paid duties rather than declare a date.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes plans before field robots arrive around 2039.
At about **71**, I expect to focus on whether work can end, not a new machine career.
think: My **knees** and retirement budget matter more now than the distant field robot date.
We need **monthly figures** before promising that regular shifts can stop.
do: **Review** household bills, savings and retirement income with my partner this year.
**Keep** repair shifts while knees and wages allow until an affordable exit date is clear.
feel: **Calm** about AI timing, careful about the household sums.
S4.quote: A line robot arriving when I am about 71 worries me less than a retirement budget with a hole in it.
fieldNote: She sees 2039 as **after fieldwork**, while refusing an unsupported retirement promise.
The next step is a **household income review**, not early retirement or a course enquiry.

steps.text: Review household bills savings and retirement income with partner this year
Keep repair shifts while knees and wages allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots could reach our poles around 2031, when I might still need the line wage. Written crew plans and actual retirement-income figures would help us see whether I can keep working or move to paid ground inspections.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who walks the wet field when a robot's map stops at the orchard gate. That knowledge needs a wage while I am working. My knees may dislike the climb, but I can still show a younger lineworker the safe route to a power pole.

headlineQuote: My knees may dislike the climb, but I can still show a younger lineworker the safe route to a power pole.
portrait: **Priya**, 58, repairs rural power lines after a vocational apprenticeship, with sore knees and retirement in sight.
She has **never used AI** and trusts her knowledge of farm tracks and safe climbing routes.
Her **three-month savings**, partner's furniture repair income and some nearby utility crews give limited room for a wage gap.
Fast field robots make her **anxious** before retirement is funded; longer timelines shift her focus to paid ground work and household sums.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots around 2031 while she still needs lineworker pay.
whatWouldHelp: Written **crew plans** and retirement-income figures would show whether she needs repairs or paid ground inspection work.
